name: brídeóg

attributes.attribute: puppet made of plaited green rushes, its name meaning little Brigit
represents St. Bridget, who took on traits of the goddess Brigit
carried from house to house on the eve of Brigit's day
demanded pennies for poor Biddy in the procession

sources: Danaher, Kevin. *The Year in Ireland*. Cork: Mercier Press, 1922, 24.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The brídeóg is a symbolic object. The name means little Brigit. It is a puppet said to represent St. Bridget. That Christian figure took on many traits of the goddess Brigit. Workers built it from two plaited clusters of green rushes. They formed a small square from the plaiting. Rushes drawn together and bound made the body. A second cluster formed the hands. The whole was dressed in rags. Sometimes it was a broom or churn-dash. A turnip served for its head. Children carried the effigy from house to house. This happened on the eve of Brigit's day. That day was the ancient Celtic feast of Imbolc. The children demanded pennies for poor Biddy. In many villages only unmarried girls carried it. In other places boys and girls took part in the procession.

okr.objective: Explain the bride og as the little Brigit effigy of the Imbolc procession.
key_results: The brídeóg is an effigy whose name means little Brigit.
It was built from plaited green rushes and dressed in rags.
Children carried it on the eve of Brigit's day, the feast of Imbolc.
Only unmarried girls could carry it in many villages.
okr.evidence: Monaghan 2008, s.v. 'brídeóg'; Danaher 1972, 'The Year in Ireland'.
